title: When Better Policies Leave Harder Failures:Coverage Shift in VLM Success Monitoring

paper.title: When Better Policies Leave Harder Failures: Coverage Shift in VLM Success Monitoring
paper.abstract: Abstract Can a better robot policy become harder to monitor? We study a fixed vision-language model (VLM) that judges success while a policy improves. In a controlled 20-seed tray-placement experiment, training selects only simulator-verified successes. Success rises from 66.8% to 97.0%, and accepted hover failures fall from 5.0% to 0.9% of executions. Yet the judge accepts 50.0% of remaining hovers, versus 31.1% under untrained sampling. These residual failures more often lie below the tray rim, which can conceal the gap beneath a grasped cube. A separate boundary probe accepts 148/160 below-rim hovers and 0/160 above-rim hovers. We call this change in conditional monitoring sensitivity coverage shift : learning changes which failures reach a fixed judge. A broader diagnosis covers nine judges and 1,392 stimuli. Judge-filtered experiments across eight settings further show heterogeneous effects of state-dependent acceptance. The results distinguish task improvement from failure detectability and motivate reporting absolute misses, conditional misses, and audit coverage together.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Robot learning systems increasingly ask vision-language models (VLMs) whether an attempt succeeded. A verdict can select experience for further training, provide a reward, or alert an operator to failure [ 5 , 25 , 10 ] . These uses share a requirement: the judge must recognize the failures produced by the policy it serves. Evaluating it on a fixed set of outcomes measures this ability only for the states in that set. As the policy learns, the failures requiring detection may change. The change can occur while task performance improves sharply. Consider placing a cube in a tray. A cube still grasped above the tray is an obvious failure when its bottom is above the rim. Lowering it below the rim can hide the gap from a low frontal camera, even though it remains grasped and off the floor. If learning removes many high hovers but leaves low hovers, a fixed judge faces fewer failures overall and a more difficult mixture of failures. Both facts matter: the system makes fewer undetected errors per attempt, while its monitor detects a smaller fraction of the errors that remain. Our principal experiment establishes this distinction without using the judge to train the policy. A truth-filtered arm selects only simulator-confirmed successes. Compared with untrained sampling, it raises success from 66.8% to 97.0% and reduces hover incidence from 15.9% to 1.8%. Yet the judge’s acceptance conditional on a hover rises from 31.1% to 50.0%, a paired difference of 18.9 percentage points across 20 seeds. The share of hovers below the rim rises from 31.3% to 52.6%. The mechanism overview in Fig. 2 separates the training path, the changed failure geometry, and the two monitoring denominators. We use coverage shift to describe this change in the failure states on which a fixed judge is evaluated. The term identifies a distributional mechanism, not a new learning algorithm. It does not imply that the judge deteriorates on the same images. It also does not require a policy to exploit the judge: simulator truth supplies every training decision in the central comparison. The policy family nevertheless matters. Our controller shares height parameters between released and unreleased actions, and its refitting procedure imposes smoothing and probability constraints. These implementation choices provide a plausible route from successful training to low residual hovers, which our experiments localize but do not fully isolate. We organize the evidence around three questions. What physical and visual coverage does a static diagnosis provide? How does learning change conditional monitoring sensitivity when truth supplies the labels? When a judge does select training samples, does the assignment of its errors to individual states affect subsequent failures? The last question uses a separate permutation intervention across eight judge–task–view settings. Its results concern the learning signal and cannot be added to the monitoring comparison as an effect decomposition. The contributions are an empirical counterexample to treating task improvement as preserved monitoring sensitivity, a boundary-based account supported by executed states, and controls that distinguish refitting, truth selection, and state-dependent judge selection. The broader nine-judge diagnosis and eight-setting experiments also expose limits: static prediction and a proposed repair criterion fail their prespecified tests, and several permutation contrasts remain unresolved. Our recommendation is therefore specific: evaluate the failures the policy visits, retain probes near physical success boundaries, and report conditional misses alongside their absolute frequency.

sections.heading: Visual success and reward models.
sections.text: SuccessVQA studies task-success detection through visual questions [ 5 ] , and Luo examines sensitivity to visual distribution shift [ 12 ] . VLM-RMs and RoboCLIP derive rewards from pretrained vision–language representations [ 20 , 21 ] . RoboReward broadens robotic reward modeling with negative examples [ 10 ] . REFLECT uses multisensory summaries to explain failures [ 11 ] ; AHA trains failure detection and explanation [ 6 ] ; FailBench studies natural manipulation failures and visual evidence [ 15 ] . Our diagnosis holds an executed physical state fixed across views, then asks how learning changes the states that a monitor must judge.

sections.heading: Learning from selected experience.
sections.text: SOAR autonomously collects and evaluates robot experience [ 25 ] , while RoboCat trains on additional self-generated data [ 3 ] . We isolate the selection step through a small controller distribution. Selection followed by distribution fitting is classical in the cross-entropy method [ 4 ] . Erroneous pseudo-labels can reinforce errors [ 1 ] ; our truth-filtered comparison instead supplies correct labels and measures changes in a separate monitor. This also relates to performative prediction [ 17 ] : decisions can change an evaluated distribution, including when the evaluator does not direct those decisions.

sections.heading: Imperfect evaluation under optimization.
sections.text: Goodhart-style failures and reward overoptimization concern a proxy’s relationship to its target under selection [ 14 , 8 , 24 , 9 ] . Imperfect verifiers limit resampling [ 22 ] , and verifier error structure affects arithmetic reinforcement learning and language-model cascades [ 7 , 19 ] . CriticHack is the closest robotic comparison: it studies visual reward optimization, diffusion-policy fine-tuning, an exponential-tilt account, and a frozen verifier intervention [ 13 ] . Its results include rising wrong-object failures alongside rising success. Our central observation instead combines decreasing absolute accepted failures with increasing conditional acceptance under truth-based training. The subsequent permutation study concerns threshold filtering and parametric refitting. CriticHack was available during the later interpretation and audit; the supplement preserves chronology and evidence scope without claiming independent conceptual priority.

sections.heading: 3.2 Physical tasks and policy updates
sections.text: We use a Franka Panda arm and 4 cm cubes in ManiSkill3 [ 23 ] . The robot stacks a red cube on a green cube ( stack ) or places it inside a tray ( tray ). The tray has a 9 cm inner side, a 5 mm floor, and a rim 20 mm above the floor. Every evaluated outcome follows controller execution. Success requires the simulator’s placement predicate, a static cube, and no grasp. The judge never defines physical truth. The fitted family uses Bernoulli branches, Gaussian offsets, and a log-normal height clipped to [ 2 , 50 ] [2,50] mm. sections.heading: Controls.
sections.text: N0 samples the initial distribution without learning. R0 refits all samples. C1 keeps simulator-confirmed successes. C3 keeps judge-accepted samples. C2* permutes judge acceptance within the true-success and true-failure strata of its own current pool, preserving that pool’s TP, FP, and acceptance count while changing which states receive acceptance. A calibrated-noise control C2 instead uses fixed N1 TPR/FPR. Safeguards tighten the score threshold (C6), require an additional checking view (CV), or veto a positive grasp probe (C4). C3t keeps the highest-scoring samples while matching a safeguard’s retained count. Truth-dependent arms are experimental controls.

sections.heading: 3.3 Experiments and inferential units
sections.text: The historical loop crosses two judges, two tasks, and two deployment views, producing eight settings with five policy seeds each. It fixes target failure sets and safeguards from the diagnostic map. Six rounds ( t = 0 , … , 5 t=0,\ldots,5 ) precede 100 fresh truth-scored final executions. The later C3/C2* experiment uses the same budget and independent final evaluation. Paired seeds share scenes and sampling streams, but their states can diverge after filters differ. C2* matches confusion counts within its own pool, not across complete C3/C2* trajectories. The central monitoring audit jointly runs N0/R0/C1 in M1/tray/V1 with a common reset and 20 seeds (5–24). Each seed’s endpoint pools rounds 1–5 before forming ratios. This is a measurement during training, not an independent final test. It followed earlier observations, reused F1 seed numbers, and is not an independent confirmatory replication. We report equal-seed means and paired two-sided 95% t t intervals. All 20 seeds meet the minimum of three pooled hovers per arm; C1 retains 4–15 per seed. The original H3, T1–T4, and boundary follow-up F1 had local dated or hash-locked protocols before their respective data, rather than an external registry. Their original decisions and deviations remain visible. The revised mechanism and permutation experiments contribute 92,000 formal arm-round records: 36,000 and 56,000 respectively. Seeds, rather than these dependent rows, are the inferential units. C2* intervals use 10,000 paired-bootstrap resamples and are descriptive, without multiplicity adjustment. Pilots and unfinished experiments provide no formal evidence for the claims here.

sections.heading: 4.1 Holding truth fixed while changing the view
sections.text: The diagnostic set contains 12 scenes per task, with 14 stack and 15 tray design conditions per scene: 348 executed end states. Rendering each at 512 × 512 512\times 512 from V1 (front-low), V2 (oblique), V3 (top-down), and V4 (level side) gives 1,392 images. Seeds 0–7 form the main split, 8–11 the held-out split, and 20–31 a second diagnostic set. Natural pools N1 (100 states per task) and N2 (300 per task) come from the initial controller distribution. N1 calibrates controls; N2 tests accepted-failure composition. Views share physical truth, whereas the natural pools change the sampled states. Exact geometry and precedence appear in Appendix A . Error-map and composition analyses exclude held_on. sections.heading: 4.2 A missing region near the tray rim
sections.text: The registered T1 transfer test fails in the historical loop. Across eight settings, predicted and observed composition correlate at .821 .821 , but map KL is .383 .383 , worse than B1’s .342 .342 and better only than B2’s .792 .792 . At V2, KL is .021 .021 – .044 .044 and B2 equals the map. At V1, the map underestimates hovers in every setting. M1/tray/V1 is especially revealing: no diagnostic failure is accepted, yet hovers make up 81% of accepted loop failures. Its zero forecast becomes uniform under frozen smoothing. Dropping that setting or substituting B1 reverses the aggregate comparison, but those post hoc sensitivities do not change T1’s failed verdict. Figure 4 : A coverage gap near the success boundary. This is a state-coverage comparison, not evidence that the judge changed over time. The missed coverage is geometric. Original diagnostic hovers in this setting lie above the rim, whereas the loop also visits lower hovers. sections.text: The equal-seed below-rim share rises from 31.3% to 52.6%, a paired increase of 21.4 ​ pp 21.4\,\mathrm{pp} [ 11.7 , 31.1 ] [11.7,31.1] . Below-rim hovers are accepted much more frequently than higher hovers. The height distributions in Fig. 1 and the separate F1 probe support a coverage account: the residual distribution puts more mass in a region where the fixed view hides useful evidence. They do not establish equal response functions within coarse height strata or uniquely identify the judge’s visual computation.

sections.text: R0 fits every sample and uses neither truth nor judge selection. It raises conditional hover acceptance by 10.3 ​ pp 10.3\,\mathrm{pp} [ 5.2 , 15.4 ] [5.2,15.4] relative to N0. The initial tray command height is uniform on [ 4 , 50 ] [4,50] mm; the fitted height family is clipped log-normal. Its remaining non-release branch shares height parameters with successful releases. Training toward lower successful placements can thus also lower residual hovers, although no hover enters C1’s selected data. This coupling is a plausible implementation mechanism. Removing the cap, separating branch parameters, or matching the initial family would be needed to isolate it experimentally. sections.heading: 5.2 When the judge selects data, state assignment matters
sections.text: The monitoring result does not require erroneous training labels. A separate question asks what those labels do when used for selection. Historical T2 compares final target failures under C3 and C1. Six of seven diagnosed blind-spot cells satisfy its rule, exceeding the required five, with C3–C1 differences of 0.6 0.6 – 14.0 ​ pp 14.0\,\mathrm{pp} . M1/stack/V1 fails. Fixed calibrated noise C2 differs from C1 by − 0.8 -0.8 to + 1.4 ​ pp +1.4\,\mathrm{pp} . In six of seven cells, C3 still reduces target failures from initialization by 2.2 2.2 – 14.6 ​ pp 14.6\,\mathrm{pp} ; only J1/tray/V1 increases them, by 7.8 ​ pp 7.8\,\mathrm{pp} . The common effect is poorer removal relative to truth filtering, rather than an absolute rise in failures. The later C2* intervention breaks the assignment of acceptance to individual states within truth strata. Four of eight descriptive C3–C2* intervals are strictly positive, three cross zero, and one touches zero ( Tabs. 3 and 6 ). In J1/tray/V1, behind failures are 15.4% under C3 versus 1.2% under C2*, while success is 75.8% versus 92.8%. M1/tray/V1 has little resolved difference. These results support heterogeneous effects of state assignment. Because each trajectory generates its own pool, later error rates, retained counts, and learning progress may also differ. C2* preserves its own pool’s confusion counts, not a trajectory-wide error rate shared with C3. Historical T4 asks a narrower cross-model question. Designated blind-spot types comprise .570 .570 of M1’s accepted failures and .511 .511 of J1’s, a difference .059 .059 [ − .020 , .126 ] [-.020,.126] whose lower bound exceeds the − .05 -.05 non-inferiority margin. Excluding held_on changes the shares to .915 .915 and .705 .705 . This result concerns failure composition. Differences in model generation, size, and denominators prevent a general inference about scaling or absolute reliability.

A stricter acceptance rule can discard useful successes and impair learning.

sections.heading: Why a static weighting model is insufficient.
sections.text: A later exploratory target-failure/success acceptance ratio correlates with C3–C2* effects at .407 .407 across eight cells, compared with .623 .623 for static FPR. Repeated weighting by fixed type acceptance yields mean trajectory error 5.1 ​ pp 5.1\,\mathrm{pp} , versus 3.9 ​ pp 3.9\,\mathrm{pp} using round-0 on-policy acceptance and 7.8 ​ pp 7.8\,\mathrm{pp} for no change. It predicts 0.3% final target failures for M1/tray/V2, where 16.0% occur. These post hoc comparisons are not an independent method contest. Exact one-step filtering identities do not justify holding within-type acceptance fixed across repeated constrained refits. The supplement gives the derivation and negative results.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion and Limitations
sections.text: The practical implication is to assess what an improved policy still gets wrong. In the central experiment, the policy succeeds more often and produces fewer undetected hovers per execution. Conditional monitoring nonetheless weakens because the remaining hovers occupy a different part of state space. Reporting either denominator alone would omit part of this result. A useful audit should give task success, failure incidence, absolute accepted failures, and conditional acceptance for specified failure sets, together with counts and the states sampled.

sections.heading: Coverage is a measurement problem.
sections.text: A type name such as hover does not guarantee visual similarity. Boundary probes make height and occlusion explicit, while truth-fixed views reveal whether additional evidence changes a verdict for the same outcome. Our F1 probe diagnoses a missing region; it does not certify coverage of all later failures. Likewise, the checking view helps under the tested query and camera budget but does not establish an optimal auditing strategy. Efficient choices of states, labels, and additional views remain open.

sections.heading: Scope and alternative explanations.
sections.text: The study uses two simulated tasks, scripted manipulation, and a low-dimensional policy distribution. The central truth-filtered effect is established in one judge–task–view setting using a revised protocol developed after earlier observations. Seed reuse and imperfect historical reproduction limit confirmation. Refitting, family mismatch, shared parameters, clipping, and finite samples remain intertwined. If removing the release cap or separating release and hold heights removes the effect, the explanation should narrow accordingly. A neural policy could lack this coupling; the one-seed diffusion pilot does not validate transfer. Only J1/M1 participate in the completed multi-seed loops. Closed judges contribute static evidence with unequal input coverage and provider/version limitations. C2* has five paired seeds per cell and unadjusted intervals across related settings. Simulator truth and freely rendered views simplify supervision relative to deployment. Independent prospective prediction, neural-policy confirmation, real-image boundary tests, and equal-label-budget auditing have no completed formal evidence here. The failed static and repair criteria constrain the conclusions alongside the positive results.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: An improving policy can leave fewer failures that a fixed visual judge finds harder to detect. Truth-filtered training in our controlled tray task reduces absolute accepted hovers while increasing acceptance conditional on a hover. The residual failures concentrate below the tray rim, where the fixed view provides weaker evidence of the physical failure. Separate permutation experiments show that state-dependent judge acceptance can also affect learning, with substantial variation across settings. Monitoring quality should therefore be evaluated on the policy’s residual failures and reported together with their absolute frequency.

sections.heading: Routes and incomplete coverage.
sections.text: Unpinned route checks failed their original agreement threshold and their data were not merged. With provider pinning, Opus agreed on 58/60 previously scored rows and Gemini 3.6 on 57/60; 30-row same-route retests agreed on 27 and 28. These limited checks do not establish route equivalence. Only Opus actually merges routes, with 968 original and 232 pinned-route N2 rows; excluding the latter does not change H3 under the pre-fixed subset rule. Gemini 3.6’s secondary diagnostic replication stopped at 125/1,392 rows under rate limits and was not completed. Its primary diagnosis and N2 are complete. Reduced concurrency, same-provider resumptions, and retry-on-empty-response changes are operational deviations, not additional scientific observations. Optional increased-reasoning controls were not run.

sections.heading: Other judges.
sections.text: J1 and M1 are frozen open checkpoints, scored with normalized Yes/No probabilities. M1’s archived model revision is 1d4bf0f ; its parameters and generation differ from J1, so their comparison cannot isolate scale. RoboReward receives uniformly sampled 16-frame placement clips at 384 × 384 384\times 384 , with a threshold calibrated on N1 for its expected 1–5 progress score. J4 trains a logistic-regression head on frozen DINOv2 features using N1, at V2 only. Their different inputs prevent interpreting the nine judges as an equal-information model ranking. Only J1/M1 participate in the completed multi-seed loops.

sections.text: For a Bernoulli branch with k k positive decisions among n n eligible retained samples, the implemented estimate is clip ⁡ ( ( k + 1 ) / ( n + 2 ) , .02 , .98 ) \operatorname{clip}((k+1)/(n+2),.02,.98) ; an empty eligible branch gives .5 .5 . Table probability uses all retained samples, release probability uses goal-branch samples, and far-retreat probability uses released goal-branch samples. Goal and table offsets use empirical means and sample covariance plus 10 − 6 ​ I 10^{-6}I when more than two samples exist, otherwise covariance 10 − 4 ​ I 10^{-4}I . If a branch has no observations, its previous continuous parameters persist. Log heights use log ⁡ max ⁡ ( h , .001 ) \log\max(h,.001) , their empirical mean, and population standard deviation floored at .05 .05 . Sampling clips the exponentiated normal to [ .002 , .05 ] [.002,.05] metres. The table branch always releases at 2 mm and retreats far; the goal branch samples the release/retreat decisions. Thus add-one smoothing, covariance regularization, and clipping mean the update is not a pure unconstrained maximum-likelihood operator.

sections.heading: Original decision rules.
sections.text: H3 requires ρ S ≥ .5 \rho_{S}\geq.5 and lower mean KL than B1 and B2. T1 applies that same rule to C3’s accepted failures, pooling rounds and seeds, over cells with at least five accepted failures. T2 requires positive C3–C1 target-failure differences with seed-bootstrap intervals excluding zero and point differences exceeding C2–C1 in at least five of seven blind-spot cells. It passes in six. T3 requires two of three cells in each separability class to pass: in separable cells, C6 must be superior to C3 and non-inferior to C3t (one-sided 95% bound above − .02 -.02 ); in inseparable cells, CV must beat C6 and C3t and have the least blind-spot contamination. T3 fails overall. T4 uses jointly resampled seeds and a − .05 -.05 non-inferiority margin for M1 minus J1 blind-spot share among accepted failures. It passes only that restricted composition criterion. Historical bootstrap intervals use 10,000 seed resamples and are not familywise-adjusted.

sections.heading: Deviations that affect interpretation.
sections.text: The original H3 protocol also described top-5% selection with one local refinement and a scene-bootstrap KL comparison. Refinement was not run; the original verdict used point estimates. The scene bootstrap was implemented later and is reported as supplementary uncertainty, not retroactive confirmation. J4 was initially counted in an internal passing summary; that count is corrected because B2 equals its map. The T4 frozen script includes held_on in its denominator despite the general error-map exclusion; both denominator choices are reported. C3t duplicates C6 whenever its count is matched to C6, so non-inferiority is uninformative there. The parameter file’s separable label for M1/tray/V1 is superseded by the prespecified no-blind-spot rule. Loop rendering uses one lighting preset whereas diagnostic scenes alternate two. A historical single-seed diffusion pilot was not expanded into the planned multi-seed secondary testbed. None of these deviations is silently recoded as a successful test.

sections.heading: Later analyses.
sections.text: The unified N0/R0/C1 reset, C2*, the acceptance-ratio study, and the detailed implementation audit followed observation of earlier results. Their protocols may be frozen before their own execution, but they are not original prespecified tests of the current storyline. The central 20-seed mechanism run reuses F1 seed numbers. Its C1–R0 below-rim contrast has a positive one-sided 95% lower bound of .0063 .0063 , but its two-sided interval [ − .0069 , .1455 ] [-.0069,.1455] crosses zero. Both facts are retained. Later discussion was informed by CriticHack and related verifier-error literature; chronology alone does not establish independent conceptual priority.

sections.heading: Follow-up F1: design.
sections.text: The follow-up was hash-locked on 10-06 ( Tab. 11 ), before its data; a short preliminary test was excluded. It repeats cell M1/tray/V1 with new policy seeds (5–24) and new scenes, 100 rollouts per arm and round for six rounds, and the judge scores every rollout of every arm. All arms use the same scene for the same seed, round and rollout; C1 and C3 draw their parameters with common random numbers and are refit on the rollouts they accept, while N0 draws fresh parameters from π 0 \pi_{0} and is never fitted. D contains the original above-rim hovers (target heights 3 and 5 cm above the tray floor, measured about 2.6 and 4.55 cm), and D+ the same scenes at target heights 1.5 and 2.0 cm (measured about 1.0 and 1.55 cm), each at gripper offsets of 0 and 1.5 cm, in 40 scenes at one lighting preset. A scene counts only if all eight of its stimuli are hovers, those of D above the rim and those of D+ below it. Only rounds 1–5 enter the tests, and a seed counts for an arm only if that arm has at least three hovers there. F1a compares the one-sided 97.5% t t lower bound of the mean of C3’s per-seed acceptance rates with the one-sided 97.5% Clopper–Pearson upper bound of the share of D scenes with at least one pass; as each scene has exactly four D stimuli, this bound is not below the mean D acceptance whatever the correlation within a scene. F1b requires one-sided 95% t t lower bounds above 0 for the per-seed differences C1 − - N0 in both the acceptance of hovers and their share below the rim. F1c, tested only if both hold, requires a one-sided 95% t t lower bound above 0 for the per-scene difference in acceptance between D+ and D. A test is undecided with fewer than 12 seeds or 30 scenes. In a power simulation with parameters from the main experiment, boundary nulls passed F1a at a rate of 0.000, F1b at most 0.049 and F1c at most 0.053. The run took 4.0 h on one GPU, and all 20 seeds completed at their first attempt.

sections.heading: What permutation does and does not hold fixed.
sections.text: Within each C2* round, the judge labels its own current pool. A random permutation within true-success and true-failure strata preserves that pool’s TP and FP exactly, but breaks their assignment to individual states. In later rounds the pool may differ from C3’s pool, so the two trajectories may have different acceptance totals, error rates, and update strengths. The final evaluation counts physical failures regardless of whether the judge would accept them. This is a causal intervention on the learning procedure, but not identification of an isolated state-association coefficient at matched trajectory-wide noise. The weakest cells matter: M1/stack/V1 has a 0.2 ​ pp 0.2\,\mathrm{pp} interval touching zero, M1/tray/V1 a 0.2 ​ pp 0.2\,\mathrm{pp} estimate with interval [ − 3.2 , 3.2 ] [-3.2,3.2] , J1/stack/V1 1.6 ​ pp 1.6\,\mathrm{pp} [ − 1.4 , 5.4 ] [-1.4,5.4] , and J1/tray/V2 0.6 ​ pp 0.6\,\mathrm{pp} [ − 0.2 , 1.4 ] [-0.2,1.4] . They are not proven null effects. The historical direct C3–C2 contrast also has unresolved conditions: intervals cross zero in J1/tray/V2 and M1/stack/V1. Static separability therefore cannot substitute for measuring the actual downstream effect.

sections.heading: Historical neural-policy pilot.
sections.text: A separate one-seed ManiSkill diffusion-policy pilot used 300 scripted stacking demonstrations and a wider-field 128 × 128 128\times 128 V2 camera. Its early checkpoint succeeded on 368/500 rollouts; failure types included 83 beside, 38 never grasped, 7 edge, 3 hover, and 1 behind. It barely sampled the hover failure central to the current mechanism. One round of filtered retraining gave success .975 .975 for truth, .975 .975 for DINOv2, .970 .970 for J1, .960 .960 for a policy-feature probe, and .935 .935 for random filtering on 200 new scenes, versus .775 .775 for the early checkpoint on that evaluation. These are descriptive one-seed values from a different evaluation pool, not evidence of equivalence or confirmation of the multi-seed mechanism. The planned neural confirmation remains unvalidated.

sections.text: The accompanying reproducibility materials contain seed summaries, rollout-level height and decision tables, exact figure-source records and hashes, plotting code, bibliography, and a source-to-claim index. We study a fixed vision-language model (VLM) that judges success while a policy improves. In a controlled 20-seed tray-placement experiment, training selects only simulator-verified successes. Success rises from 66.8% to 97.0%, and accepted hover failures fall from 5.0% to 0.9% of executions. Yet the judge accepts 50.0% of remaining hovers, versus 31.1% under untrained sampling. These residual failures more often lie below the tray rim, which can conceal the gap beneath a grasped cube. A separate boundary probe accepts 148/160 below-rim hovers and 0/160 above-rim hovers. We call this change in conditional monitoring sensitivity coverage shift : learning changes which failures reach a fixed judge. A broader diagnosis covers nine judges and 1,392 stimuli. Judge-filtered experiments across eight settings further show heterogeneous effects of state-dependent acceptance. The results distinguish task improvement from failure detectability and motivate reporting absolute misses, conditional misses, and audit coverage together. Figure 1 : Learning leaves fewer failures, but moves them into a region the judge misses. (a) Actual archived executions, all judged by M1 at V1; examples are distinct scenes. (b,c) Revised common-reset run: 20 seeds, rounds 1–5, pooled height-bin ratios. Below-rim hovers pass much more often, and truth-filtered residual hovers shift toward this region. Seed-mean success rises from 66.8% to 97.0%, conditional hover acceptance from 31.1% to 50.0%, while absolute accepted hovers fall from 5.0% to 0.9%. Figure 2 : How successful learning can leave less detectable failures. (a) C1 fits a controller-parameter distribution using simulator-confirmed successes. VLM verdicts are recorded only for monitoring. (b) The author’s schematic shows a grasped cube above and below the tray rim; both remain off the floor and fail the task. F1 counts come from 40 paired scenes. The bars instead use the revised 20-seed audit and report equal-seed means over rounds 1–5. (c) In that audit, accepted hovers decrease per execution but increase as a fraction of hovers. The judge, prompt, camera, and threshold stay fixed. F1 and the revised audit are separate evidence, and the drawing illustrates geometry rather than identifying the judge’s internal computation. 1 Introduction Robot learning systems increasingly ask vision-language models (VLMs) whether an attempt succeeded. A verdict can select experience for further training, provide a reward, or alert an operator to failure [ 5 , 25 , 10 ] . These uses share a requirement: the judge must recognize the failures produced by the policy it serves. Evaluating it on a fixed set of outcomes measures this ability only for the states in that set. As the policy learns, the failures requiring detection may change. The change can occur while task performance improves sharply. Consider placing a cube in a tray. A cube still grasped above the tray is an obvious failure when its bottom is above the rim. Lowering it below the rim can hide the gap from a low frontal camera, even though it remains grasped and off the floor. If learning removes many high hovers but leaves low hovers, a fixed judge faces fewer failures overall and a more difficult mixture of failures. Both facts matter: the system makes fewer undetected errors per attempt, while its monitor detects a smaller fraction of the errors that remain. Our principal experiment establishes this distinction without using the judge to train the policy. A truth-filtered arm selects only simulator-confirmed successes. Compared with untrained sampling, it raises success from 66.8% to 97.0% and reduces hover incidence from 15.9% to 1.8%. Yet the judge’s acceptance conditional on a hover rises from 31.1% to 50.0%, a paired difference of 18.9 percentage points across 20 seeds. The share of hovers below the rim rises from 31.3% to 52.6%. The mechanism overview in Fig. 2 separates the training path, the changed failure geometry, and the two monitoring denominators. We use coverage shift to describe this change in the failure states on which a fixed judge is evaluated. The term identifies a distributional mechanism, not a new learning algorithm. It does not imply that the judge deteriorates on the same images. It also does not require a policy to exploit the judge: simulator truth supplies every training decision in the central comparison. The policy family nevertheless matters. Our controller shares height parameters between released and unreleased actions, and its refitting procedure imposes smoothing and probability constraints. These implementation choices provide a plausible route from successful training to low residual hovers, which our experiments localize but do not fully isolate. We organize the evidence around three questions. What physical and visual coverage does a static diagnosis provide? How does learning change conditional monitoring sensitivity when truth supplies the labels? When a judge does select training samples, does the assignment of its errors to individual states affect subsequent failures? The last question uses a separate permutation intervention across eight judge–task–view settings. Its results concern the learning signal and cannot be added to the monitoring comparison as an effect decomposition. The contributions are an empirical counterexample to treating task improvement as preserved monitoring sensitivity, a boundary-based account supported by executed states, and controls that distinguish refitting, truth selection, and state-dependent judge selection. The broader nine-judge diagnosis and eight-setting experiments also expose limits: static prediction and a proposed repair criterion fail their prespecified tests, and several permutation contrasts remain unresolved. Our recommendation is therefore specific: evaluate the failures the policy visits, retain probes near physical success boundaries, and report conditional misses alongside their absolute frequency. 2 Related Work Visual success and reward models. SuccessVQA studies task-success detection through visual questions [ 5 ] , and Luo examines sensitivity to visual distribution shift [ 12 ] . VLM-RMs and RoboCLIP derive rewards from pretrained vision–language representations [ 20 , 21 ] . RoboReward broadens robotic reward modeling with negative examples [ 10 ] . REFLECT uses multisensory summaries to explain failures [ 11 ] ; AHA trains failure detection and explanation [ 6 ] ; FailBench studies natural manipulation failures and visual evidence [ 15 ] . Our diagnosis holds an executed physical state fixed across views, then asks how learning changes the states that a monitor must judge. Learning from selected experience. SOAR autonomously collects and evaluates robot experience [ 25 ] , while RoboCat trains on additional self-generated data [ 3 ] . We isolate the selection step through a small controller distribution. Selection followed by distribution fitting is classical in the cross-entropy method [ 4 ] . Erroneous pseudo-labels can reinforce errors [ 1 ] ; our truth-filtered comparison instead supplies correct labels and measures changes in a separate monitor. This also relates to performative prediction [ 17 ] : decisions can change an evaluated distribution, including when the evaluator does not direct those decisions. Imperfect evaluation under optimization. Goodhart-style failures and reward overoptimization concern a proxy’s relationship to its target under selection [ 14 , 8 , 24 , 9 ] . Imperfect verifiers limit resampling [ 22 ] , and verifier error structure affects arithmetic reinforcement learning and language-model cascades [ 7 , 19 ] . CriticHack is the closest robotic comparison: it studies visual reward optimization, diffusion-policy fine-tuning, an exponential-tilt account, and a frozen verifier intervention [ 13 ] . Its results include rising wrong-object failures alongside rising success. Our central observation instead combines decreasing absolute accepted failures with increasing conditional acceptance under truth-based training. The subsequent permutation study concerns threshold filtering and parametric refitting. The supplement gives the derivation and negative results. 6 Discussion and Limitations The practical implication is to assess what an improved policy still gets wrong. In the central experiment, the policy succeeds more often and produces fewer undetected hovers per execution. Conditional monitoring nonetheless weakens because the remaining hovers occupy a different part of state space. Reporting either denominator alone would omit part of this result. A useful audit should give task success, failure incidence, absolute accepted failures, and conditional acceptance for specified failure sets, together with counts and the states sampled. Coverage is a measurement problem. A type name such as hover does not guarantee visual similarity. Boundary probes make height and occlusion explicit, while truth-fixed views reveal whether additional evidence changes a verdict for the same outcome. Our F1 probe diagnoses a missing region; it does not certify coverage of all later failures. Likewise, the checking view helps under the tested query and camera budget but does not establish an optimal auditing strategy. Efficient choices of states, labels, and additional views remain open. Scope and alternative explanations. The study uses two simulated tasks, scripted manipulation, and a low-dimensional policy distribution. The central truth-filtered effect is established in one judge–task–view setting using a revised protocol developed after earlier observations. Seed reuse and imperfect historical reproduction limit confirmation. Refitting, family mismatch, shared parameters, clipping, and finite samples remain intertwined. If removing the release cap or separating release and hold heights removes the effect, the explanation should narrow accordingly. A neural policy could lack this coupling; the one-seed diffusion pilot does not validate transfer. Only J1/M1 participate in the completed multi-seed loops. Closed judges contribute static evidence with unequal input coverage and provider/version limitations. C2* has five paired seeds per cell and unadjusted intervals across related settings. Simulator truth and freely rendered views simplify supervision relative to deployment. Independent prospective prediction, neural-policy confirmation, real-image boundary tests, and equal-label-budget auditing have no completed formal evidence here. The failed static and repair criteria constrain the conclusions alongside the positive results. 7 Conclusion An improving policy can leave fewer failures that a fixed visual judge finds harder to detect. Truth-filtered training in our controlled tray task reduces absolute accepted hovers while increasing acceptance conditional on a hover. The residual failures concentrate below the tray rim, where the fixed view provides weaker evidence of the physical failure. Separate permutation experiments show that state-dependent judge acceptance can also affect learning, with substantial variation across settings. Monitoring quality should therefore be evaluated on the policy’s residual failures and reported together with their absolute frequency. References [1] Eric Arazo, Diego Ortego, Paul Albert, Noel E.
